JSON: Name: human_utricle_early_response_atlas Title: Single-cell and bulk RNA-sequencing atlas to define non-sensory cell heterogeneity and the early ototoxic damage response in the adult human utricle Short Hypothesis: A transcriptionally distinct supporting-cell subpopulation in the adult human utricle upregulates an injury-responsive gene program within 24 hours after gentamicin exposure (including EDNRB and MMP9) that causally promotes initiation of hair-cell regeneration markers. Related Work: Existing work includes single-cell and bulk transcriptional profiling of mouse utricle during development, maturity, and after damage, and a small number of human utricle transcriptomic datasets. Prior mouse studies resolved hair cell subtypes, SC-to-HC transitions, and injury-associated regulators (e.g., ATOH1-driven reprogramming), but they reveal species-specific marker differences and regenerative outcomes. Human studies are limited by small sample numbers, low sequencing depth, and sparse early-timepoint damage profiling; they report some conserved markers but lack resolved supporting-cell subtypes and integrated bulk/scRNA analysis of early ototoxic response. Limitations across prior approaches are: reliance on non-human models with imperfect marker conservation (hindering translation), under-sampling of rare supporting-cell subpopulations, absence of coordinated bulk and single-cell early-damage timepoints in human tissue, limited validation of druggable targets, and insufficient functional perturbation data to test causal links between early transcriptional responses and regenerative initiation. Abstract: Balance disorders lack regenerative treatments because the cellular composition and early damage response of the adult human utricle are poorly characterized. We propose to generate an integrated single-cell and bulk RNA-sequencing atlas of the adult human utricle and to map the transcriptional programs activated within 24 hours of aminoglycoside ototoxic injury. Using patient-derived utricles, we will identify and validate supporting-cell subtypes, including an SC-like population, define hair-cell subtype markers, and quantify early damage-induced differential expression at cell-type resolution. We will combine computational integration, trajectory analysis, and targeted in situ and protein validation to nominate transcription factors and druggable targets (e.g., EDNRB, MMP9, ANKRD1). The main contribution is a cell-type-resolved reference of steady-state and acute-injury states of the human utricle that reveals candidate molecular entry points for promoting endogenous regeneration. Expected outcomes include validated subtype markers, a prioritized list of early-response druggable targets, and functional perturbation experiments that test causal links between early transcriptional programs and nascent hair-cell marker induction. Experiments: Datasets: patient-derived adult human utricles collected during translabyrinthine surgery (n=6 for scRNA: 2 untreated, 2 vehicle control 24h, 2 gentamicin 24h; target total ≥2,000 high-quality cells after QC) and matched bulk RNA-seq samples (n=6; 3 control, 3 gentamicin-treated 24h). Integrate with published human utricle dataset(s) to reach ≥3,000 integrated cells. Baselines: (1) published human utricle scRNA datasets; (2) mouse utricle scRNA atlases (P6, P100) for cross-species comparison. Library prep and sequencing targets: 10x Chromium v3 aiming ≥50k reads/cell; bulk libraries 100 bp paired-end, ≥30M reads/sample. Preprocessing and QC: cell filtering (cells with MT% > 15% removed), doublet removal, genes detected >3 cells. Integration: RPCA-based integration (Seurat SCTransform + IntegrateData). Clustering: SNN clustering, UMAP visualization. Differential expression: Wilcoxon rank-sum (scRNA) and DESeq2 (bulk); FDR < 0.05 and abs(log2FC) > 0.25 (scRNA) or >1 (bulk). Key analyses: identify supporting-cell clusters and SC-like cluster; quantify percent and mean expression of EDNRB, MMP9, ANKRD1, CRYAB per cluster; compute marker specificity AUROC. Trajectory: Slingshot and Monocle pseudotime from supporting-cell clusters to early-responding SC. Validation assays: RNAscope and immunofluorescence for CALB1, SCGB2A1, EDNRB, MMP9, ANKRD1, SLPI on n≥5 independent utricles; quantify transcripts per nucleus by automated particle analysis normalized to nuclei count; statistical tests two-tailed Welch t-test, p<0.05. Functional perturbation (causal test): organotypic cultures (gentamicin 2 mM, 24h) treated with EDNRB antagonist (BQ-788) or MMP9 inhibitor versus vehicle, n≥5 per arm; endpoints: bulk and scRNA for early-response genes, percent nascent hair cells (MYO7A+/SOX2-), proliferation markers (MKI67); compare by DESeq2 and Wilcoxon; evaluate effect sizes and 95% CI. Ablation/comparison studies: (A) computational ablation removing SC-like cluster before DEG enrichment to measure loss of regeneration-related signatures; (B) temporal comparison 24h vs 48h gentamicin for dynamics of early-response program. Evaluation metrics: clustering ARI across replicates, percent variance explained by treatment (PCA), number of DE genes, FDR, AUROC for markers, change in nascent HC counts and proliferation marker expression (fold-change and p-value). Risk Factors and Limitations: Sample availability and heterogeneity: limited access to fresh adult human utricles, variable donor age/disease states, and small cohort sizes may reduce statistical power and introduce confounding. Low RNA yield and sequencing depth: inner-ear tissues yield low RNA and low gene detection per cell, limiting sensitivity to detect low-abundance transcripts and rare cell states. Batch and integration artifacts: variable sample handling and small sample counts increase risk of batch effects that confound biological signal despite RPCA correction. Causal inference limits: transcriptional correlation does not prove functional causation; pharmacological inhibitors may have off-target effects and organotypic culture may not reproduce in vivo conditions. Treatment dosing and culture artifacts: gentamicin concentration and culture conditions may cause non-physiological responses. Cross-species translation: marker and pathway divergence between mouse and human may limit applicability of functional priors. Computational scalability: integration and trajectory analyses across multiple datasets require significant compute and careful parameter selection; results can be sensitive to clustering and differential expression thresholds. Ethical constraints: limited ability to obtain longitudinal human samples or to perform in vivo manipulations restricts validation depth.
